title: She Bit a Conductor to Keep Her Seat

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

beats.text: She bit a conductor to keep her seat.

overlays.hook: She *bit a conductor* to keep her seat.

beats.text: She was born enslaved in Mississippi in 1862.

visual.sub: born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi

beats.text: As a young schoolteacher, she took a train in Tennessee and sat in the ladies' car.
The conductor ordered her into the smoking car.

visual.title: Move
visual.sub: to the smoking car, the conductor said

beats.text: She refused. When he grabbed her, she bit his hand.
It took the conductor and two other men to drag her off the train.
She sued the railroad, and won 500 dollars.
Then the state supreme court took it away.
So she picked up a pen, and became a journalist in Memphis.
In 1892, a mob murdered three Black store owners in Memphis. She investigated, and printed the facts.

visual.title: Memphis, 1892
visual.sub: she investigated, and printed the facts

beats.text: A mob destroyed her newspaper office. She could never go home again.
From Chicago, she spent her life exposing lynching.

visual.caption: Ida B. Wells with her children, Chicago, 1909

beats.text: In 2020, she was awarded a Pulitzer Prize. Eighty-nine years after she died.
They took her seat, her paper, her city. Never her voice.
Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

facts.claim: When the conductor tried to remove her from the ladies' car, Wells bit his hand ('I fastened my teeth in the back of his hand').
Born enslaved in Holly Springs, Mississippi, 1862.
A young teacher, she rode a train in Tennessee and sat in the ladies' car.
facts.note: Year: 1884 (MT, most sources) or 1883 (NPS); the reel gives no year.

facts.claim: Ordered to move to the smoking car.
The conductor and two other men removed her.
facts.note: TSM: 'with the help of other passengers'.

facts.claim: She sued and was awarded $500 by the circuit court.
The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the award.
facts.note: Year differs (1885 NPS, 1887 others); not stated.

facts.claim: Became a journalist and co-owner of the Memphis Free Speech.
In 1892 a mob murdered the three Black owners of People's Grocery in Memphis; Wells reported on it.
A mob destroyed the Free Speech office; she could not return to Memphis.
She moved to Chicago and continued her anti-lynching work.
Posthumous Pulitzer Prize special citation, May 2020; she died in 1931.

notUsed: 'The three men were her friends' (one checked source): not used.
